q: A bat hunts moths and other insects about a centimetre in size. Why is the frequency of its calls tens of kilohertz and not, for example, $1\,\text{kHz}$?
a: From an object much smaller than the wavelength only a very weak echo returns, because the wave bends around it. At the frequency $50\,\text{kHz}$ the wavelength in air is $\tfrac{343\,\text{m/s}}{50\,000\,\text{Hz}} \approx 7\,\text{mm}$, which is of the order of the size of an insect, but at the frequency $1\,\text{kHz}$ it is about $34\,\text{cm}$, tens of times greater, so only a very weak echo would return from an insect.

q: Why can a tsunami that is only about a metre high in the ocean rise to many metres high at the coast?
a: The speed of a tsunami is $v = \sqrt{gh}$, so in the shallow water near the shore the wave slows down. The back of the wave catches up with the front, the wavelength shortens and the energy is concentrated in a smaller amount of water, so the height of the wave grows.
